items.explanation: Pitt won colonial cooperation by putting recruitment under colonial assemblies and promising London would reimburse their war expenses — respecting colonial sensitivities instead of commanding them.
options: A. Threatening reprisals by the British army
B. Threatening to leave colonists to fight France alone
C. Placing colonial troop recruitment in colonial hands
D. Paying colonial soldiers generous cash bonuses
items.stem: William Pitt persuaded the colonies to fight hard in the Seven Years' War by

option_explanations.A: Pitt did not threaten the colonies with reprisals. His whole strategy was conciliation: he courted the assemblies rather than commanding them, because threats would only deepen colonial resistance.
option_explanations.B: Pitt did not threaten to abandon the colonists. He did the opposite, promising that London would back the war effort and reimburse colonial expenses.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Pitt won colonial cooperation by placing troop recruitment in the hands of the colonial assemblies and promising that London would reimburse their war expenses — respecting colonial sensitivities instead of issuing orders.
option_explanations.D: Pitt did not pay colonial soldiers cash bonuses. The financial deal he struck was with the colonial assemblies — reimbursement of their war costs — not bonuses for individual soldiers.

items.explanation: Earlier parliamentary duties had been indirect taxes on trade. The Stamp Act was Parliament's first direct, internal tax on the colonists — paper, documents, dice — and it ignited the cry of 'no taxation without representation.'
options: A. It imposed massive new duties on colonial trade
B. It was Parliament's first-ever duty touching the colonies
C. It stripped revenue from colonial legislatures
D. It was Parliament's first direct tax on the colonists
items.stem: The Stamp Act enraged the colonies because

option_explanations.A: The Stamp Act was not about massive new trade duties. Parliament had long regulated colonial trade; what was new was a direct tax on the colonists themselves, and that novelty — not the size of any duty — caused the fury.
option_explanations.B: Parliament had imposed duties touching the colonies before — the Navigation Acts and the Molasses Act of 1733, for example. The Stamp Act was the first direct internal tax, not the first duty of any kind.
option_explanations.C: The act did not strip revenue from colonial legislatures. It bypassed them by having Parliament tax colonists directly, but the assemblies kept their own taxing power.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Earlier parliamentary levies had been indirect duties on trade. The Stamp Act was Parliament's first direct, internal tax on the colonists — on paper, legal documents, dice, and the like — and it ignited the cry of 'no taxation without representation.'

items.explanation: In 1768 Adams denounced the Townshend duties as violations of the colonists' 'natural and constitutional rights,' making him the leading ideological voice of resistance in Massachusetts.
options: A. Benjamin Franklin
B. John Hancock
C. Samuel Adams
D. Patrick Henry
items.stem: Who called British taxes on the colonists 'infringements of their natural and constitutional rights'?

option_explanations.A: Franklin was in London in 1768 serving as a colonial agent; the 'natural and constitutional rights' phrasing belonged to the Massachusetts radicals' campaign against the Townshend duties, not to him.
option_explanations.B: Hancock was a wealthy merchant and organizer of boycotts, but the ideological phrasing of colonial rights was Adams's work, not his.
option_explanations.C: Correct. In 1768 Samuel Adams denounced the Townshend duties as 'infringements of their natural and constitutional rights,' making him the leading ideological voice of resistance in Massachusetts.
option_explanations.D: Patrick Henry was Virginia's great orator — famous for the Stamp Act Resolves of 1765 and 'Give me liberty or give me death' in 1775 — but this 1768 Massachusetts phrase was Adams's, not his.

items.explanation: Far from shirking, the colonies raised nearly 24,000 men — almost as many as Britain's 25,000 regulars — so British complaints about colonial ingratitude rang hollow and bred mutual resentment.
options: A. The British resented how few colonists had aided the war effort
B. British soldiers were quartered in colonial homes
C. The British resented colonial trade with the French
D. Militiamen resented British officers' condescension
items.stem: After the Seven Years' War, British-colonial resentment grew for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. The colonies raised nearly 24,000 men, almost as many as Britain's 25,000 regulars, so the British could not fairly complain that colonists had shirked the fighting; the mutual resentment came from other causes.
option_explanations.B: This was a real source of resentment: quartering British soldiers in colonial communities — formalized in the Quartering Act of 1765 — angered colonists who had to house and feed them.
option_explanations.C: This was a real British grievance: London resented colonists who traded with the French West Indies even during the war, putting profit above the imperial cause.
option_explanations.D: This was a real source of resentment: colonial militiamen, Washington among them, bridled at the condescension of British regular officers who treated them as inferiors.

items.explanation: The 1774 Congress was still moderate: John Adams brokered a compromise firmly resisting taxation without consent while stopping short of the total boycott or military preparations that radicals wanted.
options: A. Demanded a total boycott of all British goods
B. Resolved to firmly resist taxation without their consent
C. Began seriously planning military action
D. Demanded Britain stop regulating colonial trade entirely
items.stem: Most delegates to the First Continental Congress (1774)

option_explanations.A: The Congress did not demand a total boycott. It created the Continental Association — a measured, phased program of commercial resistance — but stopped short of the total immediate boycott the radicals wanted.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 1774 Congress was still moderate: it firmly resolved to resist taxation without colonial consent while stopping short of radical measures like a total boycott or military preparations.
option_explanations.C: The First Congress began no military planning. Serious military preparations came only with the Second Continental Congress in 1775, after Lexington and Concord.
option_explanations.D: The Congress did not demand an end to all trade regulation. Delegates still accepted Parliament's right to regulate imperial commerce; their fight was against taxation without representation.

items.explanation: Dickinson's 'perpetual jealousy' means unceasing popular vigilance against any 'further acquisition' of power by government -- the people must watch their rulers the way a free state watches a standing army. He is describing a civic duty of watchfulness, not envy, intercolonial suspicion, or hostility to government itself.
options: A. Envy of Britain's commercial wealth
B. Suspicion of the other American colonies
C. Constant vigilance by the people against encroachments on their rights
D. Hostility toward all forms of government
items.stem: In the passage, Dickinson's phrase 'perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty' refers to
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Dickinson is not talking about envying Britain's wealth. In eighteenth-century usage, 'jealousy' meant watchful vigilance, not envy — the sentence is about guarding liberty, not coveting riches.
option_explanations.B: Dickinson expresses no suspicion of the other colonies. His 'jealousy' is directed at government power that might encroach on rights, not at fellow Americans.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Dickinson's 'perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty' means constant, unceasing vigilance by the people against any encroachment on their rights — a civic duty of watchfulness in a free state.
option_explanations.D: Dickinson is not hostile to government itself. He writes within the tradition of mixed government and believes good government is possible — it simply must be watched.

items.explanation: Dickinson was the great conciliator: he wrote the Letters to resist the Townshend duties, yet in 1776 he opposed the Declaration of Independence and abstained from the vote, still hoping for reconciliation within the empire. His patriotism stopped at the brink of separation.
options: A. believed Parliament had a right to tax the colonies
B. He still hoped for reconciliation with Britain within the empire
C. He feared an invasion by France
D. He served as a royal official in Pennsylvania

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Dickinson did not concede Parliament's right to tax. The whole point of the Letters was that the Townshend duties were unconstitutional — taxation without representation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Dickinson was the great conciliator: he wrote the Letters to resist the Townshend duties, yet in 1776 he opposed the Declaration of Independence and abstained from the vote, still hoping for reconciliation with Britain within the empire.
option_explanations.C: Dickinson expressed no fear of a French invasion. His hesitation about independence came from hope for reconciliation, not from fear of France.
option_explanations.D: Dickinson was not a royal official. He was a Pennsylvania lawyer and assemblyman — a patriot leader, not a crown appointee.

items.explanation: Dickinson frames colonial liberty as the birthright of Englishmen -- 'the texture of their constitution' -- continuing the argument colonists had pressed since the Stamp Act crisis: Parliament was violating rights that no Englishman could be denied. The claim was inheritance, not invention.
options: A. The divine-right theory of monarchy
B. The mercantilist defense of imperial trade regulation
C. The colonial claim to the traditional rights of Englishmen
D. The Great Awakening's evangelical individualism
items.stem: Dickinson's argument in the passage most directly continues which earlier colonial tradition?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Divine-right monarchy is the opposite of Dickinson's argument. He appeals to constitutional liberty and the people's vigilance, not to a king's God-given authority.
option_explanations.B: Dickinson is not defending mercantilist trade regulation. He is attacking the Townshend duties — the very imperial economic controls mercantilism justified.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Dickinson frames colonial liberty as the inherited birthright of Englishmen — 'the texture of their constitution' — continuing the argument colonists had pressed since the Stamp Act crisis: Parliament was violating rights no Englishman could be denied.
option_explanations.D: The Great Awakening was the evangelical religious revival of the 1730s–1740s, a different tradition from Dickinson's constitutional argument about rights and government.
